Port Forwarding — vazhi & Inspector Port Links

Features·seedling·proposed·JUL 24, 2026

vazhi, a standalone multi-host ssh forward manager (drishti-style app), plus live openable port chips for every terminal in the Inspector.

Agents constantly start dev servers, and the URL scrolls away into the scrollback. This feature answers the one question kolu can’t answer today — where is the thing the agent just ran? — with exactly one concept: listening TCP ports, attributed to their terminal, one click from your browser.The inspiration, kero.sh, also shows a process list with CPU% and memory. We drop processes from the plan entirely (KISS): CPU% is the most expensive part to build for the least payoff, and a name+pid list is decoration. The process-subtree walk survives only inside the scanner, as the mechanism that attributes a port to a terminal. It ships as two things: vazhi (Tamil: way, passage) — a standalone forward manager, an app of its own in the drishti mold — and a live Ports section in kolu’s Inspector built on top of it.

The plan is built for kolu’s real deployment shape: the server runs on a headless Linux box (pureintent) while the browser runs elsewhere (zest, a macbook on the tailnet). So “open this port” never means localhost — a reachable endpoint always lives on the kolu server host, and the client builds URLs from window.location.hostname, the same name the browser already uses to reach kolu.

vazhi — a forward manager that stands alone

vazhi is the PRT0 deliverable and the reason this plan has a phase 0: like drishti for the surface stack, it is a real app with its own users that keeps the capability honest — not a kolu-internal module. It lives at packages/vazhi/ as a workspace package with its own flake.nix, to be externalized into its own repo later; in-repo first, so it can import surface-remote’s ControlMaster helper directly and skip the drishti-style pair-PR burden until the API settles.

One model, two mechanisms. vazhi owns a map of forwards, N hosts × N ports — (host, remotePort) → local listener — where every listener binds a non-loopback address on the machine vazhi runs on:

  • Remote host → ssh -L *:61000:127.0.0.1:5173 <host> — added and removed on a live multiplexed connection via ssh -O forward / ssh -O cancel, no new handshake.
  • Kolu-host loopback → a plain TCP relay (0.0.0.0:61000 → 127.0.0.1:5173), no ssh involved. Needed because even the server host’s own loopback is unreachable from a viewer on another machine.

The ssh side needs no connection management of its own: controlMaster.ts computes the ControlPath deterministically from the destination and ControlMaster=auto makes whoever connects first the master. vazhi uses the same controlOptPairs helper, so standalone it creates its own masters, and alongside kolu it silently shares the mirror’s sockets — the ControlPath convention is the integration, with zero coordination code.Forwards die with their master connection, so a dropped host can never leak tunnels; vazhi’s own cancel path handles the deliberate case.

One binary, serve-or-attach. There is no separate daemon/CLI/TUI trio — vazhi is a single executable and the first one to run becomes the resident: it serves the forwards state over a @kolu/surface app (dogfooding the same stack kolu consumes), owns the relays, and — when it has a TTY — renders a kaval-tui-style live table. Every later invocation attaches to the resident as a client: vazhi in a terminal is the TUI face, vazhi add pu-dev:5173 · vazhi ls · vazhi rm pu-dev:5173 are one-shot verbs, and kolu supervises a headless (TTY-less) resident on the server host. The socket arbitration is not new invention — surface-daemon-supervisor exists precisely to decide who owns the socket, the kaval pattern.The lifetime semantics fall out naturally: run standalone, the TUI is the resident, and closing it closes your tunnels — the same intuition as closing a hand-rolled ssh -L. Run alongside kolu, the kolu-supervised resident holds the forwards and the TUI is a mere viewer, so closing it severs nothing. vazhi is mechanism only — create, cancel, list, pick a free port, self-clean. Every policy decision (when to forward, when to auto-cancel, what to show) belongs to its consumers.

Security posture, stated: a vazhi listener is unauthenticated raw TCP on the kolu server’s serving interface — anyone on the tailnet can connect, the same exposure as running the dev server on 0.0.0.0 yourself. That is the accepted v1 trust model (the tailnet is the trust boundary, as it already is for kolu’s own UI); per-forward auth would be a later, separate feature.

FORWARDED PORTS

$ vazhi ls
pu-dev:5173 → 0.0.0.0:61000  ssh · up 4m
zest:8080   → 0.0.0.0:61003  ssh · up 1m

A Ports section joins the existing blocks in packages/client/src/right-panel/MetadataInspector.tsx (pure rendering — the data arrives on the terminal’s metadata like everything else). The flows:

  • Open. Click a chip → window.open on http://${location.hostname}:…, matching the Code tab’s external-open idiom (CodeTab.tsx:1114). Wildcard-bound ports on the kolu server host open directly on their own port — no forward. Loopback-bound and remote ports go through vazhi: the client calls create, gets the listener port, opens it, and the chip gains a ⇄ :61000 badge. Forwarding is lazy — first click only, never eager for every detected port.An agent session can hold six listening ports; auto-tunneling all of them VS-Code-style keeps idle listeners alive for ports nobody opens. Lazy costs one ssh -O forward round-trip (~ms on the multiplexed socket) on first click. This also covers the corner where the terminal’s host is the viewer’s machine (zest as a kolu remote host, viewed from zest): traffic loops zest → pureintent → ssh → zest — roundabout but correct, and not worth a special case in v1.
  • Manage. A Forwarded Ports group lists every active vazhi forward — host:remotePort → :localPort, origin auto (chip click) or manual, cancel ⨯ per row. Kolu auto-cancels an auto forward when the scanner sees its remote port die; manual forwards persist until cancelled or their host disconnects.
  • Manual forward. The ＋ Forward a port… row and a ⌘+K command accept host:port — for a port the scanner missed or one outside any terminal’s subtree.
  • Discoverability. One tip in settings/tips.ts: “Click a port in the Inspector to open the server an agent just started.”

Detection: ports, attributed to the terminal

Process facts belong to the PTY owner, so the scanner is a new module in kaval — packages/kaval/src/processScan.ts, beside the existing foreground sampler (ptyHost.ts:620). One host-wide pass every 5 secondsCadence and the unref’d, non-overlapping poll shape copy packages/padi/src/memorySampler.ts and its derived.cell(source({ read, install: everyMsOr(…) })) wiring in servePadi.ts:247. builds the pid→ppid table once, partitions it into per-shell subtrees, and joins listening TCP sockets against each subtree:

  • linux — pid table from /proc/*/stat; LISTEN rows (with their bind address) from /proc/net/tcp + tcp6, joined to pids via /proc/<pid>/fd socket-inode readlinks — the same technique surface-daemon-supervisor/src/socketHolder.ts:100 uses for unix sockets.
  • darwin — ps -axo pid,ppid,comm for the table; lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -P -n -F pcn for ports, under a hard timeout and SIGKILLed if wedged, as socketHolder.ts:157 does. Both platforms gate CI; the darwin path is day-one work.

Each terminal’s sample — PortInfo { port, name, wildcard } in packages/terminal-vocab/src/schema.ts, beside ForegroundSchema:145 — is deduped by structural equality before publishing on the ptyHostSurface contract, so an unchanged scan emits nothing: the churn guard that keeps a 5-second ticker from thrashing SolidJS. From there every layer exists: the padi sensor set folds it into TerminalSnapshot, the surface serves it (snapshot-then-deltas invariant, .claude/rules/streaming.md), and the reconcile-backed store in useTerminalMetadata.ts:180 delivers leaf-grained ticks to the section.

Architecture verdicts, conditioned on this build: the scanner is a leaf module inside kaval — a bounded one-shot scan with kaval as its only consumer — and graduates only if it grows independent consumers or its own streaming volatility. The forward manager is the opposite case: ssh connection/forward lifecycle is a hard volatility with genuinely independent consumers (interactive standalone use, one-shot verbs, kolu), which is exactly why vazhi is an app of its own rather than a module in kolu’s server — one binary with a serve-or-attach rule, not three artifacts.

Build plan — the PRT track

id ships needs proof
PRT0 vazhi: one serve-or-attach binary (TUI · headless · verbs) · own flake.nix — standalone forward on a real remote box, no kolu running
PRT1 kaval scanner · Ports section · direct open — e2e: spawned listener’s chip appears + opens
PRT2 kolu ⇄ vazhi: lazy forward · Forwarded Ports UI · manual · auto-cancel PRT0 + PRT1 real remote box: chip → tunneled HTTP 200 via shared master
PRT3 embedded in-kolu preview pane PRT2 deferred — not planned yet

PRT0 and PRT1 are independent and can proceed in parallel; only PRT2 needs both.

PRT0 — vazhi (one PR)

Package with its own flake.nix (nix run .#vazhi): the single serve-or-attach binary — resident (surface server + relays, TUI when it has a TTY, headless when not) and client verbs. Done when, with no kolu running: vazhi add <box>:5173 against a real remote box (pu harness) prints the listener port, curl http://<vazhi-host>:<port> from a different machine returns the remote server’s body (proving the non-loopback bind), vazhi rm tears it down, and a vazhi TUI attached to the same resident shows the row live — proving serve-or-attach, not just serve. Plus the socket-sharing proof: with kolu’s mirror connected to the same host, vazhi add must create no second ssh master (assert one master via ssh -O check + process count) — the criterion the ControlPath-convention design exists to satisfy.

PRT1 — detection + Ports section (one PR)

Scanner, ports schema field, sensor fold, the Inspector section, direct-open chips, the tip. Done when an e2e scenario runs node -e 'require("http").createServer((_,r)=>r.end("ok")).listen(8123,"0.0.0.0")' in a real kolu terminal and asserts the 8123 chip appears within two scan ticks and clicking it opens the page at location.hostname:8123 — pinning the real path (kaval scan → ptyHostSurface → padi snapshot → surface → reconcile store), which no client-side mock can satisfy. Parser unit tests run on fixture /proc trees and fixture lsof -F pcn output; the darwin gate (aarch64-darwin) must be green, not skipped. Loopback-bound chips render with a “needs a forward” affordance that activates in PRT2.

PRT2 — kolu ⇄ vazhi (one PR)

Kolu supervises the vazhi daemon, consumes its surface; chip click → lazy create; tunnel badges; Forwarded Ports group; manual forward + ⌘K command; auto-cancel policy. Done when, verified with the remote-host-testing harness against a real remote box and a viewer on a different machine than the kolu server: clicking a remote terminal’s chip creates the forward through vazhi over the shared ControlMaster socket (a second ssh connection does not satisfy this), the opened http://<kolu-host>:<localPort> returns the remote server’s body, cancelling the row severs it, and stopping the remote server auto-cancels the auto forward within two scan ticks. Evidence video of the click-to-page flow.

PRT3 — embedded preview (deferred)

Open the forwarded page inside kolu — a browser pane in the Code tab, in the spirit of the Codex desktop app — instead of a new tab. Explicitly out of scope until PRT2 shipsA cross-origin iframe surface for arbitrary dev servers is a genuinely bigger build, and any server sending X-Frame-Options: DENY / frame-ancestors refuses framing — the new-tab path must remain the fallback regardless.; no design here yet — when it matures this section is rewritten, not layered.
